title: Chain of Responsibility
objectives: Separate routing policy from a caller.
Trace first-handler selection and explicit rejection.
Change handler order without confusing routing with validation.

sections.heading: The problem: one job, one responsible desk
paragraphs: A small print workshop receives a Job containing a format name and a page count. Labels should go to a label desk; ordinary reports go to a general desk. The general desk can also print labels when the special desk is absent. Each job must reach at most one desk. The workshop rejects a page count below one or above one thousand before considering any desk. Unsupported formats must produce a visible unhandled result. No real printing happens in this teaching program: it chooses a destination so that routing can be checked without consuming supplies.

For two fixed destinations, an if statement is a sound start. Read the format, choose a destination, and return. There is no need to build a class family merely because several destinations exist. The limit appears when different workshop shifts need different ordered sets of rules. Copying the whole function for each shift also copies validation and fallback behavior. One shift may then accept zero-page jobs while another rejects them. We need to assemble the choices while keeping the routing contract in one place.

sections.heading: Make each choice a small, honest question
paragraphs: A handler is a piece of code that accepts a request, decides whether it can handle it, and reports that decision. A chain of responsibility is an ordered set of these handlers. The delivered program represents each handler as a function. Rule is a short name, introduced by using, for std::function<Reply(const Job&)>. This standard wrapper can hold different callable objects with the same call shape. Here the shape means: borrow a read-only Job and return a Reply. The program does not need a next pointer inside every handler because a vector already stores their order.

Reply is std::optional<std::string>: it contains either one destination string or no string. std::nullopt explicitly means there is no answer here. That is different from an answer whose string happens to be empty. The if (reply) condition asks whether a value exists. The expression *reply then accesses that value; the asterisk is safe because the presence check came first. A missing answer is ordinary control flow, not an exception. The caller receives a separate text result, unhandled, only after every handler declines.

sections.heading: Follow control and data through the chain
paragraphs: route first checks the page count. The test uses ||, meaning that either bad bound is enough to reject the job. Valid jobs enter a range-based for loop. In for (const auto& rule : rules), the colon means take each item from rules in order. auto obtains the function-wrapper type from the vector; the reference avoids copying that wrapper; const prevents this loop from changing it. The same read-only Job is borrowed by each call. No handler owns the job, stores its address, or extends its lifetime.

For a label job, label_rule returns a value, so route returns immediately. general_rule is never called for that request. For a report, the first handler returns no value and the second supplies the destination. For archive, both decline. The compiler checks that each stored callable has the required input and result shape. Which handler supplies the answer is decided during execution from the job and the order of rules. Moving the rules into a different vector can change behavior without recompiling route, although changing the source initializer still requires rebuilding the executable.

sections.heading: First-handler routing is not an all-stage pipeline
paragraphs: A pipeline is a sequence in which several stages may each perform part of the work. A document pipeline might validate pages, add a tracking code, write a record, and print. Success at one stage normally means continue. Our chain has a different rule: an answer means stop. If a maintainer converts return *reply into an assignment and continues looping, the general desk can replace the label desk because both accept labels. With real printing, that same mistake could produce two copies. The word chain alone does not tell a reader which stopping rule applies.

Decide the rule before choosing an interface. In a validation pipeline, an enum such as Continue or Reject makes sense; in this router, optional destination makes sense. Mixing both meanings in one bool makes it hard to tell whether true means finished or allowed to continue. Shared requirements such as a valid page count belong before routing. A handler that is optional in one configuration must not be the only place that enforces a mandatory check. The empty-rule test proves that having no handlers remains a defined situation.

sections.heading: Boundaries, costs, and a practical review
paragraphs: The handlers are pure selection functions: their result depends on the job, and they do not print, store files, or change outside data. This makes order tests cheap and repeatable. With n handlers, an unsupported request makes n calls; an early match needs fewer. std::function offers runtime flexibility but may allocate when storing a large callable. For this tiny fixed router, direct calls or a table of plain function pointers can cost less. Neither performance claim should replace a measurement if routing is on a busy path.

Before adding a rule in real software, inspect overlap, position, failure meaning, and ownership. A fallback placed first can hide every special case. A rule that captures a local reference and survives that local variable can later access a dead object. The current vector stores free functions, so it has no such captured lifetime. A linked chain would also need a no-cycle rule; this vector traversal has no link cycle to create. The model deliberately omits retries and external actions. Choosing a destination successfully does not prove that the destination later completed the job.

example.title: Print-workshop request routing
requirements: Reject page counts outside 1 through 1000 before routing.
Choose the first willing handler; expose unsupported formats.
Allow the same handlers to be arranged in another order.
example.design: Store small function handlers in a vector and use an optional destination. The vector makes order visible; the optional result separates a decline from an accepted request. One route function owns the stopping rule.
example.alternative: A direct if/else chain is clearer when the choices and their order never vary. Virtual Handler classes suit handlers with substantial private state, but would add unnecessary lifetime machinery to these two stateless rules.
invariants: A valid job receives at most one destination.
Every handler sees the same unchanged job.
Rejected counts never enter a handler.

failures.mistake: Continue through the vector after finding a destination.
failures.consequence: A label job can finish as general desk instead of label desk.
failures.reason: The two handlers overlap, so the last answer replaces the first.

failures.mistake: Place the general handler before the label handler.
failures.consequence: Every supported label job selects general desk.
failures.reason: The first willing handler wins even if a later one is more specific.

example.verification: The program checks label/report/unknown cases, both invalid count sides, the largest valid count, an empty chain, and reversed order. It verifies selection behavior, not print hardware or concurrent changes to rules.
example.maintenance: A new destination becomes one independently testable rule. Configuration reviews must still examine overlaps and order because individual handler tests cannot establish the whole routing policy.

diagram.title: One route, at most one destination
diagram.explanation: Flow arrows mean the next possible execution step, not ownership. Each successful handler returns to route immediately; there is no success arrow from the label desk to the general desk. The code blocks below show the early return that gives the overview this meaning.

focus.title: One handler can decline
focus.what: This function asks whether the label desk is responsible.
focus.where: route invokes it through the first Rule in the vector.
focus.why: A separate question can be reused without copying route.
focus.invariant: Declining must not create any printing side effect.
focus.risk: Returning a destination for every format prevents later rules from running.
explain: Define a handler that borrows a read-only job and returns an optional reply.
The comment explains that no reply is a deliberate decline.
Check whether the format is anything other than label.
Return the standard empty-optional marker when it is not a label.
Return a present string when the desk accepts the job.

focus.title: The stop rule lives in one loop
focus.what: This loop searches for the first present reply.
focus.where: It runs only after the page-count guard has accepted the job.
focus.why: The caller does not need to know the selected desk or the number of rules.
focus.invariant: Return at once on a present answer.
focus.risk: Replacing return with continued processing changes the contract into a different kind of chain.
explain: The comment states the first-handler policy.
Borrow each callable in vector order without changing it.
Call that rule with the same job and store its optional reply.
Check that a string is present before accessing it.
Return the string and end route immediately.
Close the loop after a decline, allowing the next rule.
Return an explicit unhandled result if no rule accepted.

trace.reason: Two pages lies inside the common valid range.
The optional contains a string; route returns it.
general_rule now gets a chance and answers general desk.
The count check ends route before any rule is called.

summary: Order is part of the routing policy.
A missing optional value expresses an ordinary decline.
One accepted handler ends this chain.
Pipelines need their own continue/stop contract.
Keep mandatory checks outside optional handlers.

exercises.prompt: Change the maximum valid page count from 1000 to 500. List the old tests that must change and two new boundary cases.
exercises.hint: Find both the guard and the check using the old upper bound.
exercises.answer: Change the guard to pages > 500. The old report with 1000 pages must now be rejected. Check 500 as accepted and 501 as rejected; retain zero-page and unknown-format tests.

exercises.prompt: In the primary main, replace the rules initializer with {general_rule, label_rule}. Predict the four printed lines, ignoring checks that deliberately assert the old order.
exercises.answer: The lines become general desk, general desk, unhandled, rejected. The first primary check would fail before printing unless updated; this separates predicting the routed values from predicting execution of an unchanged test harness.

exercises.prompt: A developer changes if (reply) to if (!reply) but leaves return *reply. Explain what happens for a report.
exercises.hint: A report produces an empty optional at the first rule.
exercises.answer: The branch now dereferences an empty optional, violating its precondition. There is no defined correct output to predict. Restore the presence test; do not describe a crash as guaranteed.

exercises.prompt: Choose between this chain and a switch for three permanently fixed format codes with no overlap.
exercises.answer: A switch is reasonable because a fixed direct mapping needs no configurable search. Choose the chain if fallback order or independently added rules is a real requirement, and test overlap explicitly.

exercises.prompt: Add an express rule for reports of at most five pages. Keep labels special and reject zero pages. State three regression cases.
exercises.hint: Insert the rule before general_rule; keep the shared guard.
exercises.answer: A five-page report selects express, a six-page report selects general, and a label still selects label. Zero pages must be rejected before the express rule can accept it. The companion lab implements this change.

exercises.prompt: Explain in three sentences why an accepted destination must not also mean the printer completed the job.
exercises.hint: Separate routing from an outside effect.
exercises.answer: Routing identifies responsibility. A printer may later be offline or run out of paper. Keep a separate delivery result and retry policy so routing success does not hide an external failure.

lab.task: Extend the starter with express_rule: reports of one through five pages choose express desk. Install it before the original rules. Preserve every original check and printed line, then print express: express desk.
checks: A report with five pages selects express desk; six selects general desk.
Labels still select label desk; zero-page reports are rejected.
lab.answer: The reference solution adds one callable and a new vector, leaving the original vector and tests intact. The central guard rejects zero before express_rule runs. Making the express rule validate pages again is harmless but duplicates policy that can drift.

glossary.definition: A callable that decides whether it is responsible for a request.
Ordered handlers with an explicit rule for passing or stopping requests.
A value wrapper that may contain one value or no value.
Stages that may each contribute work before a later stage runs.

problem_title: Route a request to the right handler

attachment_alignment.epub_section: Chain of Responsibility: ordering-system checks, contextual-help propagation, handler structure, applicability, and relations to other patterns.
attachment_alignment.intent: Send a request through an ordered set of possible handlers without making its caller select the final receiver. Each handler decides whether this request belongs to it. This chapter teaches the first-handler-wins form shown by the attached C++ sample; the EPUB also explains a validation form in which several checks run until one stops the request.
attachment_alignment.mechanism: The essential choice is handle or pass onward. The caller supplies the request and an entry point. A handler that declines allows the next handler to try. A successful handler stops this version of the chain. No handler accepting is a defined result. Order therefore affects behavior; merely calling several functions in sequence does not establish this pattern.

roles.responsibility: Give every handler the same input and a clear way to accept or decline. Rule is a callable contract, not an inherited base class.
Continue after a decline and detect the end. The original stores successor links; the new program stores order in one vector.
Apply one local acceptance rule without knowing which other rule will eventually answer.
Choose order and submit requests. Construction chooses policy; handlers implement the individual decisions.

source_walkthrough: main links MonkeyHandler to SquirrelHandler and then DogHandler. SetNext returns the successor, which permits the two linking calls to form one expression. ClientCode receives only a Handler reference and tries Nut, Banana, and Cup of coffee.

For Nut, MonkeyHandler declines by calling AbstractHandler::Handle. That base operation forwards to SquirrelHandler, which returns a nonempty answer. DogHandler receives no call for that request. For Banana, the monkey answers immediately. For coffee, every handler declines and the last base call returns an empty string.

The second demonstration enters at SquirrelHandler. Nut still finds a receiver; Banana now reaches the end untouched because the monkey is outside this subchain. The attached output demonstrates entry-point choice as well as normal success and exhaustion. MeatBall is accepted by DogHandler in the source, but the supplied client never submits it.
attachment_alignment.adaptation: The original food choices become print-job choices with deliberate overlap: both desks accept labels. This makes the effect of reordering visible. Empty-string decline becomes std::optional so absence is distinct from a real answer. A vector replaces raw successor pointers and manual deletion; route retains the same ordered delegation and stopping rule. Common page validation occurs before the optional handlers. The example returns a destination and omits actual printing, linked-chain cycles, and GUI parent traversal.
attachment_alignment.recognize: Point to both the local decline and the next-handler decision. In this program those appear in label_rule and route, respectively. Explain which request can reach no receiver and why a more general handler placed first hides a specific one. Naming a class Handler alone is insufficient evidence.

contrast.distinction: Command packages an action for later invocation. This chain decides which possible receiver should accept a request; it does not require a request object with execute().
A decorator adds behavior around a wrapped operation. This chain deliberately allows one successful handler to prevent all later handlers from running.

teach.action: Ask learners to predict the three outcomes from the monkey entry, then from the squirrel entry, before revealing Output.txt.
Mark each return that accepts and each base call that declines. Follow one coffee request to the final empty result.
Run the print example, reverse its rule vector, and ask why only the label destination changes. Then test an unsupported format and invalid pages.

checks.question: Why does Banana fail only in the supplied subchain demonstration?
checks.answer: The chosen entry excludes MonkeyHandler, its only accepting receiver. The remaining handlers correctly decline.

checks.question: Is a successful page check supposed to end this router?
checks.answer: No. It is a prerequisite. A destination answer ends routing; mixing those meanings would accidentally stop valid jobs before a desk is selected.
